Wrist drop is a common symptom of radial nerve damage. It is a result of the inability to dorsiflex the foot due to unopposed plantar flexion. Loss of sensation in the skin of the medial half of the arm suggests damage to the radial nerve as this innervates the medial side of the hand and upper arm. The ulnar nerve supplies the lateral half of the hand and upper arm so damage to this would cause loss of sensation on the lateral side of the arm. The median nerve runs down the medial side of the humerus and forearm and does not supply any sensation in the forearm. The musculocutaneous nerve innervates the anterior arm muscles so it does not innervate any forearm or hand muscles. The medial pectoral nerve is one of the branches of the internal thoracic artery so does not run anywhere near the wrist. The question is essentially about coupling, which is a key concept in physiology 1.  When a cell needs to be selective in what it lets in and out, it uses transporters.  These move things across the membrane against their concentration gradients.  However, as they do this they can create a backlog of things trying to enter/leave the cell.  If there is too much backlog, the cell will die due to osmotic changes.  To prevent this from happening, the transporters 'couple' with other transporters.  In antiporters, for every 2 things leaving the cell, 1 thing is allowed in. For symporters, for every 2 things entering the cell, 1 thing leaves.  This means that the influx of things going in matches the efflux of things coming out. 8 is the clotting factor deficiency in haemophilia A. It can be remembered as '8 - ate my gcse results' or '8-again, I'm such a failure'. Coagulation factor VIII (FVIII) is a glycoprotein involved in the secondary formation of fibrin from fibrinogen during the coagulation cascade. Deficiencies in Factor VIII result in hemophilia A, a disease which impairs blood clotting leading to uncontrolled bleeding. Symptoms include bleeding into joints and muscles, prolonged bleeding after minor cuts or during tooth extraction. Haemophilia A affects approximately one in 5,000 males worldwide. Haemophilia A is caused by a mutation in the gene coding for Factor VIII or the gene regulatory region of this gene. Haemophilia B affects mainly males and is due to deficient or defective coagulation factor IX. Haemophilia C is a rare form of the disease that affects mainly males and is due to deficiency of coagulation factor XI. Haemophilia A and B are inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. All daughters of an affected person will be unaffected, but all sons will inherit the disorder. Haemophilia C follows an autosomal recessive pattern of inheritance. This means that both copies of the gene for coagulation factor XI must be altered for a person to have the condition. Haemophilia A and B are treated by replacing Factor VIII or Factor IX concentrates into the circulation. The concentrates are purified from large pools of plasma collected from many donors. These treatments reduce the amount of bleeding and lessen the need for surgical interventions. They do not cure the disease. Risk of infection transmission has been greatly reduced since the introduction of new viral inactivation technologies. However, the risk cannot be eliminated entirely because of the nature of the production process. The answer is C - radial nerve as it innervates all of these muscles. This is because when the arm is abducted at 90 degrees (forearm parallel to the ground) the radial nerve is under tension. So if a large amount of force is applied (like being slammed to the ground), there is a high chance that the nerve will be damaged. This type of injury is called a radial head fracture. A radial nerve palsy is often associated with a humeral shaft fracture - also known as Monday morning quarterback syndrome since its often seen in football players. This means that the patient would have weaknesses such as wrist extension, elbow flexion and finger abduction. However they would still have sensation on their dorsal hand as the superficial branch of the radial nerve continues to supply this area. Patients may also experience numbness on the back of their hand due to compression of the radial nerve trunk. To diagnose this, doctors would look for signs of weakness and then check for Tinel's sign. Tinel's sign is where you tap over the affected nerve and the patient reports paresthesia. If the nerve is severely damaged, it may not be possible to elicit this sign.  A median nerve injury would result in claw hand - permanent flexion of the PIP joints and extension of the MCP joints. It would also result in wrist drop. An ulnar nerve injury would result in claw hand too but with hyperextension of the MCP joints and flexion of the PIP joints. An axillary nerve injury would result in paralysis of the deltoid and teres minor. A femoral nerve injury would result in footdrop. Puberty consists of a series of growth spurts controlled by Growth Hormone (GH). This is released as a series of pulses rather than a continuous release. These pulses are stimulated by low levels of testosterone and oestradiol. The higher these hormones get, the more frequent the pulses of GH and hence the taller the child will be during puberty. Tall children may have later peaks, shorter children earlier ones. After the peak height velocity has been reached, there is a period of consolidation where further growth occurs but at a slower rate. During this period it is important to maintain good nutrition as poor nutrition during this time could stunt final adult height.  From the lecture on puberty by Dr. Helen McCarthy. 16/10/2014. Angiotensin II increases blood pressure by vasoconstriction and also stimulates the thirst reflex. It also causes increased production of ADH from the posterior pituitary gland. However it does not cause an increase in renin secretion. Renin is secreted when blood pressure drops due to decreased GFR caused by a decrease in blood volume. This decrease in volume is usually caused by reduced fluid intake. Therefore angiotensin II acts as a negative feedback mechanism to increase fluid intake. Renin converts circulating plasma angiotensinogen into angiotensin I. Angiotensin converting enzymes (ACE) then convert angiotensin I into angiotensin II. The angiotensin II then causes vasoconstriction which increases blood pressure. It also stimulates the thirst centre in the hypothalamus causing an increase in water intake. This should compensate for any fluid loss that has caused the drop in blood volume in the first place. If this doesn't happen then the renin-angiotensin system can get stuck in a positive feedback loop whereby less blood volume causes less ADH release and less water reabsorption in the kidney, causing further drop in blood volume. This is known as dehydration and can be fatal if not treated. Treatment includes administration of IV fluids and drugs such as ACE inhibitors or angiotensin II receptor blockers that prevent the conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II. These drugs are used in heart failure and hypertension to reduce blood pressure. They do this by reducing vasoconstriction. They also have a side effect of increasing water excretion in urine. This is because they prevent angiotensin II binding to its receptors in the distal convoluted tubule of the kidneys. This prevents aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex. Aldosterone normally binds to cells in the cortical collecting duct and stimulate sodium and chloride uptake into the cell. This alters the acid/base balance of the tubular fluid and stimulates the thirst centre. The increased water intake counteracts the effects of the diuretic so that less water is excreted in urine. 10% of all fractures are scaphoid fractures. They are particularly common in young adults who fall onto their outstretched hands. They are also very slow to heal due to the scaphoid being in a unique position in the body. It is located at the base of the hand, surrounded by carpal bones and deep muscles of the forearm. This means there is little blood supply to the bone and so a blood clot cannot form to aid healing. Therefore the bone heals by new bone formation from the ends of the fracture which takes time. Pain may be experienced months after the injury as the bone continues to heal. Another reason this bone is prone to fracture is that it is one of only two bones in the body with a waisted shaft. This makes it weaker and more susceptible to torsion and twisting forces. (Taken from Radiology lecture and Student's revision guide) All other carpal bones have a square cross-section apart from trapezoid which is triangular.  If anyone wants to know why capitulum, trapezium and lunate aren't more probable answers they are less likely because they lie more proximally in the hand, making them less vulnerable to force. Also capitulum is diamond shaped not round like scaphoid.  I hope this helps! Let me know if you want any further information about scaphoid fractures. I found it really interesting. Glycine is synthesised via a folate dependent reaction, therefore D is the correct answer. Dopamine, serotonin, glutamate and GABA are all synthesised via a non-folate dependent reaction. Folic acid supplementation will not affect their synthesis. However, if there was a deficiency of vitamin B9 (folic acid), then dopamine, serotonin, glutamate and GABA synthesis could be affected. This is because they are synthesised by decarboxylation of amino acids, which requires a cofactor such as tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4). BH4 is synthesised from 5,6,7,8-tetrahydropteroyltriphosphate (tetrahydroptase) which requires the enzyme formylmethionine synthetase. Formylmethionine synthetase requires one carbon atoms from the essential amino acid metabolite methionine to form tetrahydrobiopterin, however methionine cannot cross the blood brain barrier, therefore it relies on dietary intake of folate to achieve this. If there is a folate deficiency, then BH4 will not be produced, therefore dopamine, serotonin, glutamate and GABA cannot be synthesised. This can lead to psychotic symptoms associated with a folate deficiency. Source: Neurochemistry lecture. Prostaglandins are produced by cyclo-oxygenases (COX) which have two isoforms, COX-1 and COX-2. COX-1 is constitutively expressed and produces small amounts of prostaglandins under normal conditions. COX-2 is induced by cytokines, growth factors and hormones and produces larger quantities of prostaglandins during inflammation. NSAIDs such as ibuprofen inhibit both isoforms but it is primarily COX-1 that is inhibited. Prostacyclin, PGI2 and thromboxane A2, TXA2 are all prostaglandins. Thromboxane A2 is a vasoconstrictor and stimulates platelet aggregation. Prostacyclin is a vasodilator and works against platelet aggregation. PGI2 may be procoagulant or anti-coagulant depending on the cell type producing it. NSAIDs inhibit prostacyclin production from the endothelium and so the balance in arteries favours TXA2, a vasoconstrictor, and thus promotes the likelihood of thrombosis through platelet aggregation. This increases the chance of clot formation.  Why do NSAIDs increase the risk of CV events? Arterial thrombosis is one of the most common causes of morbidity and mortality in patients with cardiovascular disease. Aspirin reduces the incidence of myocardial infarction and stroke in patients with cardiovascular disease. Aspirin works through irreversible inhibition of COX-1 and therefore does not have the same adverse effects as other NSAIDs.NSADIS also inhibit the synthesis of prostaglandins involved in mucous secretion, gastric mucosal integrity and renal blood flow and sodium excretion. PCT - Glucose and sodium move out from the blood into the tubule cells via co-transport proteins. They leave the cell on the basolateral side by simple diffusion. Thick ascending limb - Na+ is transported against its concentration gradient using the energy provided by the sodium/potassium pump. This allows water to be reabsorbed in this part of the nephron. DCT - Na+ and Cl- are co-transported, against their concentration gradients using the energy provided by the sodium/potassium pump. Water follows because of the osmotic effect. The solution in the lumen becomes more concentrated as water is removed, and more water is drawn out of the tubular fluid and into the blood. This is known as the 'Lowers's countercurrent'. This prevents blood from entering the left atrium from the right ventricle, resulting in the left atrium becoming the de facto oxygenated chamber.  Pulmonary circulation becomes established as blood passes through the open ductus arteriosus and then moves up the aorta and into the rest of the body. Also it is important to note that atropine is only short term useful as it causes desensitisation of muscarinic receptors.  In the long term other drugs must be used. This works by blocking the effects of sympathetic adrenaline.  If treatment with atenolol does not work then atropine may be added to the regimen.
